cases.court: Illinois Appellate Court, First District, Third Division
cases.role: Joined Justice Reyes's judgment and opinion; did not author a separate opinion.
cases.issue: Second Amendment challenge to conviction for carrying a firearm without a valid FOID card; notice and opportunity to respond in collateral proceedings.
cases.holding: Affirmed denial of collateral relief. The facial challenge to the FOID-related aggravated-unlawful-use-of-a-weapon provision failed because constitutional applications existed, including disarming people covered by Rahimi. The under-21 FOID challenge also failed. Dismissal without notice or an opportunity to respond violated due process, but was harmless because the legal claims could not succeed.
cases.rationale: Applied Bruen and Rahimi. Rejected the State's argument that unlicensed carrying automatically falls outside Second Amendment protection; examined historical justification. The panel rejected procedural forfeiture arguments and reached the constitutional merits.
cases.scope: Facial validity of the specific FOID-related provision, not approval of every gun restriction or a blanket ruling that all young adults can be disarmed. The separate age-only offense was not before the court.
cases.subsequentStatus: Appellate rehearing denied October 23, 2024 (official report cover). Illinois Supreme Court denied leave to appeal September 24, 2025, docket 131264, identifying First District case 1-23-0384. A discretionary-review denial is not a merits endorsement. Later federal review not verified.

sources.label: Official September 24, 2025 PLA dispositions, PDF page 5, docket 131264

comparison.status: Narrow outcome potentially comparable only to a specific firearms-licensing baseline
comparison.axis: Preserved FOID-related carrying restriction against a facial challenge
comparison.limits: Must also disclose use of Bruen/Rahimi, recognition of protected conduct, facial-challenge threshold and the author's identity. This does not establish Lampkin's personal ideology or Trump support.

cases.court: Illinois Appellate Court, First District, Third Division
cases.publication: Published precedential opinions; initial 2024 judgment reversed by Illinois Supreme Court
cases.role: Authored both the initial 2024 opinion and the 2025 opinion after Supreme Court remand; D.B. Walker and Van Tine joined both.
cases.issue: Transition from cash bail to the Pretrial Fairness Act and individualized proof needed for detention.
cases.holding: On remand, affirmed detention after independent review of the parties' proffers. Alleged threats combined with circumstantial evidence satisfied the statutory proof, dangerousness and inadequacy-of-release-conditions requirements.
cases.rationale: Applied the State's clear-and-convincing burden to all three detention elements and de novo review under People v. Morgan where the hearing relied only on proffers. Lack of prior felonies and bond forfeitures did not outweigh the particular alleged threat.
cases.scope: Pretrial detention sufficiency, not a determination of guilt or a ruling for or against cash bail as policy.

proceduralHistory.result: Lampkin's opinion reversed detention on statutory timing grounds and required a release-conditions hearing; did not decide evidentiary sufficiency.

Illinois Supreme Court reversed. Majority held the State could respond to a request to reopen unsatisfied cash-bail conditions with a detention petition, then remanded the unresolved sufficiency issues. Lampkin was not a member of that court.
proceduralHistory.pinpoints: ¶¶39–53; Rochford/O'Brien special concurrence ¶¶54–89 agreed with reversal on forfeiture/plain-error grounds but disputed the majority's statutory interpretation.

proceduralHistory.result: Lampkin authored affirmance of detention under the Supreme Court mandate.

cases.subsequentStatus: The 2024 appellate judgment was reversed. The latest merits opinion verified is the March 26, 2025 affirmance on remand. No later Watkins-Romaine disposition was found in the 101 official 2024–2026 PLA lists screened; this is not proof that all review or trial proceedings are concluded.

comparison.status: Not comparable to a general party or Trump label
comparison.axis: Statutory transition procedure and individualized detention proof
comparison.limits: Initial procedural release ruling and later detention affirmance must travel together. Following a Supreme Court mandate and evaluating alleged threats does not reveal a stance on cash-bail abolition or a general tough/soft-on-crime ideology.

cases.case: Eberhardt v. Village of Tinley Park
cases.court: Illinois Appellate Court, First District, Third Division
cases.role: Authored majority opinion; D.B. Walker and Van Tine joined.
cases.issue: Public comment at special municipal meetings; alleged retaliation through attorney-disciplinary complaints; taxpayer challenge to outside counsel.
cases.holding: Affirmed dismissal with prejudice. An agenda-germaneness rule at special meetings satisfied reasonableness and viewpoint-neutrality requirements under the Illinois Constitution; regular meetings allowed other topics. Retaliation claims failed pleading requirements. The outside-counsel claim failed for taxpayer standing and, alternatively, lawful appointment/ratification.
cases.rationale: The rule excluded off-topic comments across viewpoints. The opinion expressly recognized that state-law immunity cannot defeat a federal section 1983 claim. It found insufficient allegations of actionable retaliatory harm and, for some defendants, personal involvement.
cases.scope: Contains a substantive speech ruling plus pleading, preclusion and standing rulings. It does not authorize suppressing criticism because officials dislike a viewpoint, and it is inaccurate to describe the entire decision as only about standing.
cases.subsequentStatus: Appellate rehearing denied May 14, 2024 (official report cover). Illinois Supreme Court denied leave to appeal September 25, 2024, docket 130759, identifying First District case 1-23-0139. A discretionary-review denial is not a merits endorsement. Later federal review not verified.

sources.label: Official September 25, 2024 PLA dispositions, PDF page 14, docket 130759

comparison.status: Not comparable to a general party or Trump label
comparison.axis: Agenda-limited public-comment forum and civil-rights pleading
comparison.limits: An ordinary municipal forum rule is not a ruling on presidential power, media censorship, political dissent generally, or Trump's conduct. Viewpoint discrimination remained prohibited.

cases.case: Maksym v. Board of Election Commissioners of the City of Chicago
cases.court: Illinois Appellate Court, First District, First Division
cases.publication: Published opinion; appellate majority judgment reversed
cases.role: Lampkin dissented. Hoffman authored the majority opinion and Hall joined it. Lampkin would have left Rahm Emanuel on the mayoral ballot.
cases.issue: Whether temporary Washington service and renting out a Chicago home abandoned the candidate's Illinois electoral residency.
cases.holding: Lampkin's dissent would have affirmed the electoral board and circuit court: established residency continued absent abandonment, and the board's finding of no intent to abandon was supported by the evidence. She rejected a newly imposed actual-presence standard.
cases.rationale: Applied existing residency precedent, the challengers' burden to show abandonment and deference to supported electoral-board findings.
cases.scope: A candidate-specific statutory residency dispute. The dissent is not itself binding law; it says nothing about election fraud, certification of presidential results, or Trump eligibility.
pinpoints: Appellate slip opinion pp.25–30 (position and abandonment analysis)
cases.outcome: Dissent favored ballot access; appellate majority ordered removal
cases.subsequentStatus: On January 27, 2011, Illinois Supreme Court reversed the appellate majority and affirmed the circuit court/board, leaving Emanuel eligible. See 242 Ill. 2d 303, No. 111773, slip pp.18–21. Justices Freeman and Burke agreed with the result but disputed the majority reasoning and criticized the tone of both the appellate dissent and Supreme Court majority (pp.22–25).

sources.label: Official appellate opinion and Lampkin dissent

comparison.status: Not comparable to a general party or Trump label
comparison.limits: A Democratic candidate benefited, but deciding his residency under established law is not an endorsement of his party. This predates Trump's presidency and concerns a different legal question from election denial or presidential immunity.

verificationNotes: Official appellate index results were cross-checked against inventory-opinions-lampkin.json. Each selected opinion is listed as an Opinion and Final.

The official index notes the initial Watkins-Romaine decision as reversed by 2024 IL 130618. That year is an index error: the Supreme Court opinion itself is dated January 24, 2025 and cited 2025 IL 130618; this ledger uses the opinion.

All 101 PLA PDFs linked under 2024, 2025 and 2026 on the official Supreme Court PLA disposition page were downloaded and text-screened. Relevant matching disposition pages were inspected. These lists are not a federal citator or trial-docket check.
The ISBA short Eberhardt case digest emphasizes standing. The full opinion has distinct constitutional merits, pleading and standing holdings, accurately separated here.
